content.content:
1	Temperature-sensitive goods such as vaccines, biological samples, prepared meals and laboratory reagents are frequently shipped in insulated carriers that hold a payload within a target temperature band for a period of hours or days. Carriers of this general kind fall into two broad families. Powered carriers use a fan, a pump or another driven air mover, together with a power source, to force air over a cold source and through the payload space. Passive carriers omit the power source and rely on conduction from, and natural convection around, a refrigerant mass such as water ice, dry ice, gel packs or sealed cassettes charged with a phase-change material.
2	
3	Passive carriers are attractive because they have no battery to charge, no motor to fail and no electrical approval burden for air transport. They are also harder to control. When a refrigerant mass is simply laid on top of, beside or beneath a payload, the cooled air falls where gravity and the packing arrangement happen to send it. Items directly against the refrigerant are driven toward the cold end of the acceptable band or below it, while items on the far side of the payload sit in a stagnant warm layer. The result is a temperature spread across the payload that grows as the load is packed more densely, and that varies from shipment to shipment because it depends on how a particular packer arranged the goods and the refrigerant on a particular day.
4	
5	Attempts to impose a defined circulation path on a passive carrier run into a practical difficulty. The path is defined by clearances, by openings and by the alignment between them, and every one of those relationships is destroyed if the component that carries the openings is set down rotated, offset or skewed by a person working quickly at a packing bench. A carrier that circulates air well when it is assembled precisely, and poorly when it is not, delivers the variability it was intended to remove. Packing instructions, printed arrows and keyed corner blocks all depend on the packer looking, and none of them acts on a component that has already been set down out of position.
6	
7	Two further problems attend repeated reuse of a passive carrier. First, moist ambient air admitted each time the carrier is opened condenses on the cold surfaces of the refrigerant mass and runs down into the payload space, wetting labels and cartons and, over many cycles, leaving standing water in the base of the carrier. Where the refrigerant is a sealed cassette, drying the interior often means removing the cassette from service. Second, a passive carrier gives no account of itself. If the payload was exposed to a temperature excursion in transit, and the refrigerant has since recovered, an inspection at the receiving dock shows a cold carrier and a firm cassette, and the excursion leaves no trace. Electronic data loggers record such events but add cost, battery management and a reading step to every unit shipped, and they report a sensor location rather than the state of the refrigerant that the payload actually depends on.
8	
9	There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier that establishes the same circulation path around the payload every time it is closed, without a powered air mover and without relying on the care of the person who packed it, that manages the condensate produced by repeated opening without taking the refrigerant out of service, and that retains a visible mechanical record of a refrigerant temperature excursion after the refrigerant has recovered.
10

12	
13	Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. 14	
15	The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 positioned to align with the side supply passages 28.
16	
17	The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.
18	
19	Registration and retention by the lid
20	
21	The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into the registered position.
22	
23	This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.
24	
25	The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

27	The circulation path
28	
29	In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20.
30

Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

34

A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.
36	
37	The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

40	
41	The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. FIG. 6 shows the mechanical exposure indicator 80 as it appears from outside the outer shell 10, at the outer surface of a side wall 14. Referring to FIG. 7, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. 42

44	
45	The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.
46	
47	The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.
48	
49	Operation

At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 positioned to align with the side supply passages 28.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into the registered position.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. FIG. 6 shows the mechanical exposure indicator 80 as it appears from outside the outer shell 10, at the outer surface of a side wall 14. Referring to FIG. 7, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44. FIG. 6 and FIG. 7 show the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Essential and optional features

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

content.text: I've read all inputs, draft sections, and all seven figure briefs. Here is the review.

input.summary:
Source ledger: the disclosure and the single USER passage in input/conversation.md are identical in substance; the only other conversation passage is labelled YOU (drafting agent) and carries no authority (its account of earlier FIG. 1/FIG. 5 edits was disregarded, and the current briefs do not depend on it).

Traced clean: all thirty-one numerals in draft/numerals.md and every claim limitation map to affirmative USER text — shell/floor/side walls/upper edge, tray on feet with the lower return passage, tray side walls spaced inward forming two side supply passages, perforations, rigid spacer frame with two opposed cassettes, central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages, the full circulation path, absence of any fan/pump/powered air mover, depending indexing rib entering the mating channel and shifting the module into the registered position, gasket sealing after registration, resilient feet pressed against shell ledges, the shallow condensate channel around the tray with removable wick, pull tab and duct-lower-end discharge openings, and the irreversible latched exposure indicator that does not control airflow. Claim 12's progressive engagement is a fair inference from "gasket seals ... after registration"; claim 4's confronting faces across a central space follow from "opposed" plus the central inlet; the essential/optional split in draft/08 tracks the closing sentence of the disclosure. Formalities check out: title/applicant/inventor per brief.md, no priority claim, no government support, abstract 141 words, no means-plus-function, 3 independent claims, every table numeral illustrated on at least one figure and no figure numeral missing from the table, no placeholders or open questions, and no "by way of example"/"any closed outline" broadening in the application text (the schematic conventions stay inside the figure briefs).

Internal consistency check: line 7-7 carries the repeated designation 7 at both ends in figures/FIG-6.md, is named "line 7-7 of FIG. 6" in figures/FIG-7.md and in both sentences of draft/07-drawings.md; the FIG. 6 arrow direction is consistent with FIG. 7 showing the outer surface at the left. The three broken-line curves in figures/FIG-1.md are each designated with the enlarging figure and are matched by the "there designated FIG. 3/4/5" wording in the three enlargements and in draft/07-drawings.md; the lower-left curve list correctly excludes the floor and trough that figures/FIG-4.md does not draw. Numeral meanings are unique throughout (tray feet 22 vs. resilient feet 58; side walls 14 vs. tray side walls 26; module 40 vs. spacer frame 42).

Six findings. Two are critical untraced functional-surface geometry verbalised in the figure briefs: the runout direction of the registration slot ("groove running across the wall thickness" in figures/FIG-2.md), which fixes the direction in which the indexing rib constrains and shifts the frame; and the latch contact topology in figures/FIG-7.md ("above the shaft", "to the right of the coil spring", "lower end spaced above ... the upper surface of the shaft"), which fixes the order of latch and spring along the stem and the face the latch acts on. Two are major untraced structural relationships: the indicator body drawn through the full wall thickness "open at both of its ends" with the stem's "inner end project[ing] past the inner surface of the wall body" (the disclosure supports only outward visibility and thermal coupling, never penetration into the interior), and the spacer-frame step surface placed "above the level of the bottom panel" (the disclosure relates the resilient feet only to the shell ledges, never to the frame bottom). One minor untraced item is the wick/pull-tab placement detail in figures/FIG-5.md ("filling its lower part", "its free end lying within the trough"). One minor internal-logic defect is in draft/08-detailed-description.md, where the resilient feet are said to be "compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60" — a load path is not a structural member, so the compressing member is left unidentified.

Every fix is a deletion or a shape-neutral substitution confined to the figure brief or, for the last item, a supported rewrite of one sentence; none adds a speculative shape or optional embodiment to the application text. I did not inspect rendered images, and I did not assess patentability, novelty, validity, or the prior_art/ tracing, which are outside this preflight.

findings.title: Runout direction of the mating channel ("running across the wall thickness") is untraced functional geometry
findings.where: figures/FIG-2.md, mating-channel paragraph ("The top edge of the near long side wall carries an upwardly open groove running across the wall thickness.")
findings.detail: The brief fixes the length direction of the registration slot. The mating channel is the functional slot that receives the depending indexing rib and, on the closing stroke, translates the module into the registered position; a groove whose length runs across the wall thickness is open at the inboard and outboard faces and constrains the rib only along the wall length, whereas a groove running along the wall would constrain the perpendicular direction. Runout direction of a functional slot is substantive even where the brief calls the geometry schematic, and no USER passage states any orientation for the channel. The choice also cannot be justified as a bare outline convention because it adds a direction of constraint on which the disclosed registration depends.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "The top edge of the near long side wall carries an upwardly open groove running across the wall thickness. This groove is the mating channel 56." (figures/FIG-2.md). Nearest source, which shows the gap: "As the lid closes, the rib enters a mating channel in the spacer frame and shifts the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages." (input/disclosure.md; identical USER text in input/conversation.md). The disclosure states no orientation, length direction, or open ends for the channel; there is no affirmative passage supporting "running across the wall thickness".
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-2.md replace the sentence with: "The top edge of the near long side wall carries an upwardly open groove, shown schematically. This groove is the mating channel 56." Leave the numeral note ("56: well inside the groove in the top edge of the near long side wall.") unchanged. No change to draft/07-drawings.md, draft/08-detailed-description.md, or the claims is required, since none of them verbalises the channel's runout direction.

findings.title: Latch contact topology and latch/spring ordering in FIG. 7 are untraced
findings.where: figures/FIG-7.md, temperature-responsive-latch paragraph ("A small block sits above the shaft within the outline, to the right of the coil spring, projecting downward with its lower end spaced above and clear of the upper surface of the shaft ...")
findings.detail: The temperature-responsive latch is a functional joint. The brief verbalises which side of the stem it acts on (above, engaging the upper surface), its position along the stem relative to the spring (inboard of the coil), and the direction of its projection (downward). These are contact-topology and end-position statements, which remain substantive even where the brief says "shown schematically", and none of them is traceable to an affirmative USER passage. The depiction-convention allowance does not apply because the brief verbalises exactly the relationships the allowance excludes.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "A small block sits above the shaft within the outline, to the right of the coil spring, projecting downward with its lower end spaced above and clear of the upper surface of the shaft, the latch being shown released, shown schematically. This block is the temperature-responsive latch 84." (figures/FIG-7.md). Nearest source, which shows the gap: "An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette and retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position." (input/disclosure.md). The disclosure gives the latch's function only; it never states where the latch lies relative to the stem or the spring, which surface it engages, or in what direction it projects. The released state shown is supported by the exposed position.
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-7.md replace the paragraph with: "A small block within the outline beside the shaft, shown schematically, is spaced from the shaft, the latch being shown released. This block is the temperature-responsive latch 84." And change the numeral note to: "84: well inside the small block beside the shaft." draft/08-detailed-description.md already states only that the latch "retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position" and "is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens", so it needs no change.

findings.title: Indicator body drawn open at both ends through the full wall thickness, with the stem's inner end projecting into the interior, is untraced
findings.detail: The brief asserts that the indicator body passes through the whole thickness of the insulated shell wall and is open at both ends, and that the stem projects past the inner surface into the carrier interior. The outward projection is supported (the indicator is visible from outside and the stem moves to an exposed position), but the inward penetration of the insulated wall and the inboard projection of the stem are structural relationships with technical substance (a through-breach of the insulation, and a member reaching into the interior across the side supply passage) that no USER passage states. The disclosure asserts only thermal coupling, which it does not localise or embody in any structure.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "drawn as a horizontally elongated plain rectangular outline extending through the thickness of the wall body from its outer surface to its inner surface, is the body of the mechanical exposure indicator 80, shown schematically and open at both of its ends" and "to the left the shaft projects past the outer surface of the wall body, and to the right its inner end projects past the inner surface of the wall body" (figures/FIG-7.md). Nearest source, which shows the gap: "The shell includes a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette and retained by a temperature-responsive latch." (input/disclosure.md). There is no affirmative passage that the indicator or its stem passes through the wall, is open at its inner end, or projects into the interior.
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-7.md replace the two passages with: "Carried by the wall body, and drawn as a horizontally elongated plain rectangular outline within the outer portion of the wall body and open at its outer end, is the body of the mechanical exposure indicator 80, shown schematically." and "An elongated horizontal shaft lies within that outline and projects to the left past the outer surface of the wall body. This shaft is the indicator stem 82." Retain the numeral notes as written (82 is called out on the part of the shaft projecting left). draft/08-detailed-description.md needs no change, as it says only that the indicator is "visible from outside the outer shell 10" and "thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44".

findings.title: Height of the resilient-foot bearing surface relative to the spacer-frame bottom panel is untraced
findings.where: figures/FIG-2.md, outward-step paragraph ("its downwardly facing surface above the level of the bottom panel and outboard of it")
findings.detail: The downwardly facing surface from which the resilient feet depend is the load-transmitting face by which lid closure holds the module down on the shell ledges. Placing that face at a stated level above the frame's bottom panel is a relative-location statement about a functional load-bearing surface and is substantive notwithstanding the schematic label. The disclosure relates the resilient feet only to the ledges of the shell; it never relates the feet, the step, or their bearing surface to any part of the frame's bottom. The outboard position is supported, because feet of the frame must reach ledges projecting inward from the shell wall, but the level relationship is not.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "The lower part of each long side wall carries an outward step, shown schematically, its downwardly facing surface above the level of the bottom panel and outboard of it. Small blocks project down from that surface, two visible at the front, shown schematically. These blocks are the resilient feet 58." (figures/FIG-2.md). Nearest source, which shows the gap: "The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the shell so that the module cannot lift away from the tray during transport." (input/disclosure.md). No passage places the feet or their bearing surface at any level relative to the frame bottom.
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-2.md replace the first sentence with: "The lower part of each long side wall carries an outward step, shown schematically, having a downwardly facing surface outboard of the frame." Keep the following two sentences unchanged. figures/FIG-1.md and figures/FIG-3.md need no change, as they state only that a foot lies flattened between a downwardly facing outboard surface of the frame and the ledge, which the disclosure supports.

findings.title: Wick fill depth and pull-tab placement within the trough are untraced
findings.detail: The brief verbalises how deeply the wick fills the condensate trough and states that the pull tab runs along the trough with its free end lying inside the trough. The trough is a functional flow boundary and the tab is the disclosed means of access, so a stated fill depth and a stated in-trough end position carry technical substance beyond a generic outline. The disclosure supports the wick lying in a shallow channel and a pull tab that remains accessible when the tray is removed, but not the fill depth, the run along the trough, or the free end's location within it.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "An elongated body of absorbent material lies in the trough, filling its lower part, shown schematically. This body is the absorbent wick 72. A narrow strip, shown schematically, extends from one end of the absorbent body along the trough, its free end lying within the trough and clear of the absorbent body." (figures/FIG-5.md). Nearest source, which shows the gap: "A removable absorbent wick lies in a shallow condensate channel around the product tray. ... A pull tab on the wick remains accessible when the product tray is removed, allowing the wick to be replaced without opening a phase-change cassette." (input/disclosure.md). No passage states a fill depth or the position of the tab's free end.
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-5.md replace the paragraph with: "An elongated body of absorbent material lies in the trough, shown schematically. This body is the absorbent wick 72. A narrow strip, shown schematically, extends from one end of the absorbent body, its free end clear of the absorbent body. This strip is the pull tab 74." Change the numeral note to: "74: well inside the narrow strip extending from the absorbent body." In figures/FIG-1.md, change "a narrow strip at one end of the right-hand appearance lying in the trough" to "a narrow strip at one end of the right-hand appearance".

findings.title: Resilient feet described as compressed against a "load path" rather than a member
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md, "Registration and retention by the lid" section, sentence beginning "The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60"
findings.detail: A load path is not a structural member, so nothing can be compressed between a ledge and a load path. The sentence leaves the member that bears down on the feet unidentified and reads as an unresolved hedge, while the surrounding text and claim 2 correctly attribute the compression to closure of the lid acting through the spacer frame that carries the feet. Rewriting removes the indefiniteness without adding any structure beyond the disclosure, which states that the closing movement presses the feet of the spacer frame against the ledges of the shell.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport." (draft/08-detailed-description.md). Source: "The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the shell so that the module cannot lift away from the tray during transport." (input/disclosure.md). Claim 2 already recites "closure of the insulated lid presses the resilient feet against the ledges".
findings.fix: Replace the sentence with: "Closure of the insulated lid 60 compresses the resilient feet 58 between the spacer frame 42 and the ledges 18, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport." No change to the claims or figure briefs is needed.

structured_output.summary:
Source ledger: the disclosure and the single USER passage in input/conversation.md are identical in substance; the only other conversation passage is labelled YOU (drafting agent) and carries no authority (its account of earlier FIG. 1/FIG. 5 edits was disregarded, and the current briefs do not depend on it).

Traced clean: all thirty-one numerals in draft/numerals.md and every claim limitation map to affirmative USER text — shell/floor/side walls/upper edge, tray on feet with the lower return passage, tray side walls spaced inward forming two side supply passages, perforations, rigid spacer frame with two opposed cassettes, central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages, the full circulation path, absence of any fan/pump/powered air mover, depending indexing rib entering the mating channel and shifting the module into the registered position, gasket sealing after registration, resilient feet pressed against shell ledges, the shallow condensate channel around the tray with removable wick, pull tab and duct-lower-end discharge openings, and the irreversible latched exposure indicator that does not control airflow. Claim 12's progressive engagement is a fair inference from "gasket seals ... after registration"; claim 4's confronting faces across a central space follow from "opposed" plus the central inlet; the essential/optional split in draft/08 tracks the closing sentence of the disclosure. Formalities check out: title/applicant/inventor per brief.md, no priority claim, no government support, abstract 141 words, no means-plus-function, 3 independent claims, every table numeral illustrated on at least one figure and no figure numeral missing from the table, no placeholders or open questions, and no "by way of example"/"any closed outline" broadening in the application text (the schematic conventions stay inside the figure briefs).

Internal consistency check: line 7-7 carries the repeated designation 7 at both ends in figures/FIG-6.md, is named "line 7-7 of FIG. 6" in figures/FIG-7.md and in both sentences of draft/07-drawings.md; the FIG. 6 arrow direction is consistent with FIG. 7 showing the outer surface at the left. The three broken-line curves in figures/FIG-1.md are each designated with the enlarging figure and are matched by the "there designated FIG. 3/4/5" wording in the three enlargements and in draft/07-drawings.md; the lower-left curve list correctly excludes the floor and trough that figures/FIG-4.md does not draw. Numeral meanings are unique throughout (tray feet 22 vs. resilient feet 58; side walls 14 vs. tray side walls 26; module 40 vs. spacer frame 42).

Six findings. Two are critical untraced functional-surface geometry verbalised in the figure briefs: the runout direction of the registration slot ("groove running across the wall thickness" in figures/FIG-2.md), which fixes the direction in which the indexing rib constrains and shifts the frame; and the latch contact topology in figures/FIG-7.md ("above the shaft", "to the right of the coil spring", "lower end spaced above ... the upper surface of the shaft"), which fixes the order of latch and spring along the stem and the face the latch acts on. Two are major untraced structural relationships: the indicator body drawn through the full wall thickness "open at both of its ends" with the stem's "inner end project[ing] past the inner surface of the wall body" (the disclosure supports only outward visibility and thermal coupling, never penetration into the interior), and the spacer-frame step surface placed "above the level of the bottom panel" (the disclosure relates the resilient feet only to the shell ledges, never to the frame bottom). One minor untraced item is the wick/pull-tab placement detail in figures/FIG-5.md ("filling its lower part", "its free end lying within the trough"). One minor internal-logic defect is in draft/08-detailed-description.md, where the resilient feet are said to be "compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60" — a load path is not a structural member, so the compressing member is left unidentified.

Every fix is a deletion or a shape-neutral substitution confined to the figure brief or, for the last item, a supported rewrite of one sentence; none adds a speculative shape or optional embodiment to the application text. I did not inspect rendered images, and I did not assess patentability, novelty, validity, or the prior_art/ tracing, which are outside this preflight.

findings.title: Runout direction of the mating channel ("running across the wall thickness") is untraced functional geometry
findings.where: figures/FIG-2.md, mating-channel paragraph ("The top edge of the near long side wall carries an upwardly open groove running across the wall thickness.")
findings.detail: The brief fixes the length direction of the registration slot. The mating channel is the functional slot that receives the depending indexing rib and, on the closing stroke, translates the module into the registered position; a groove whose length runs across the wall thickness is open at the inboard and outboard faces and constrains the rib only along the wall length, whereas a groove running along the wall would constrain the perpendicular direction. Runout direction of a functional slot is substantive even where the brief calls the geometry schematic, and no USER passage states any orientation for the channel. The choice also cannot be justified as a bare outline convention because it adds a direction of constraint on which the disclosed registration depends.

(input/disclosure.md; identical USER text in input/conversation.md).
